IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: The EMC directive deals with apparatus capable of causing a disturbance or which might lose performance in the presence of an electromagnetic disturbance. The essential and mandatory requirement is that such apparatus shall not prevent other apparatus from operating as intended, and that the apparatus itself shall have an adequate level of immunity to allow it to operate as intended. This is dealt with in detail in Articles 1, 2 and 4 of the directive. The national legal requirements of the member states adopting the directive and their infringement are discussed. The use of CE marking is also mentioned as are the cases when a standard is applied. Extracts from various standards are given and immunity testing is discussed.

articleTitle: Due diligence for the small business [EMC regulations]
publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: Discusses the needs of a small business to know of the Electromagnetic Compatibility Regulations 1992 and their application. The author also considers trading standards, risk analysis and CE marking.

articleTitle: Building equipment from products with known EMC performance
publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: In order for system integrators to use EMC data derived from testing components and subsystems two areas must be addressed: common installation rules and common test conditions. Provided the above issues are addressed the modular method to compliance based on the arguments and methods described in this paper can be used within a technical construction file to show compliance with the EMC Directive (89/336/EEC).

publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: When installing equipment in a large installation the main EMC considerations are the earthing of the equipment and interconnecting cabling. Unfortunately when it comes to earthing and cabling, there is not one correct way or set of rules that will be right in every case. However, there are regulations that must be obeyed and guidelines that will ensure the optimum EMC performance for the majority of cases. This paper will concentrate on the key issues to enable them to be applied with some understanding.

articleTitle: Very low cost methods to gain confidence with emissions and immunity
publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: This paper describes how small companies may minimize their exposure to expenditure on EMC testing services and equipment. Its purpose is to show how companies making low risk equipment may gain confidence in their products EMC performance such that the CE mark may confidently be applied. The purpose of the testing described is to increase confidence in existing suppositions. These tests can not be regarded as being substitutes for testing on equipment which it anticipated will be EMC active. If a small manufacturer is making an electrically simple piece of equipment that contains no electrically nonlinear components, then by utilising the tests described the manufacturer may gain sufficient confidence in the product to place it onto the market, or into service, without unnecessary expenditure.

articleTitle: Due diligence for the small PC manufacturer
publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: Discusses the EMC Directive 89/336/EEC from the point of view of a small PC manufacturer. The author considers what is included, routes to compliance, product design, product testing and quality control.

articleTitle: The EMC directive: a pragmatic approach
publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: The EMC law stems from European Union Directive 89/336/EEC. A feel for compliance with this can be obtained by reading Article 2.1, Article 4, Article 7.1 and Article 10.2. The source of legislation within the UK is in the Electromagnetic Compatibility Regulations 1992. Two clauses in these are mentioned in particular: Clause 40 and Clause 88.

articleTitle: EMC compliance using appropriate design techniques
publicationTitle: IEE Tutorial Colloquium on EMC for the Small Business (Digest No: 1997/111)
abstract: The most usual approach to compliance with the EMC Directive is via the harmonized standards route, which involves choosing and then "applying" one or more harmonized standards from the raft of available references that have been published in the Official Journal of the EC. Those unfamiliar with EMC but used to safety requirements have quite naturally formed the view that standards specify "a way of doing things", that is to say, they are applied at the design stage of a new product as a set of rules that determine the design choices. If you follow these rules, then you have complied with the standard. EMC standards are not like this. They are standards for testing, not for design. You cannot "design to comply with" an EMC standard, you can only demonstrate that you have complied by performing the specified test. This paper discusses some of the implications of this characteristic for product designers, and recommends design approaches which will go some way towards helping to meet the problems it causes.
